extracted.intended_audience: law professors, patent scholars, patent attorneys, and policymakers interested in patent doctrine and economics
extracted.subtask_description: Scholarly analysis of how doctrines of infringement, claim breadth, and economic theories (prospect theory, common-pool models) should shape patent scope decisions across different industry patterns of technical advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subservient (blocking) patent / dominant patent relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: A broad patent can 'dominate' a narrower one, producing a subservient (narrower) patent that cannot be practiced without a license from the holder of the dominant patent; conversely the dominant patentee cannot practice the particular improved feature claimed in the narrower patent without a license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although courts may characterize an inventor's patent as subservient (often in litigation), the holder of a subservient patent still gains advantages: (1) she can exclude the holder of the broad patent from practicing her improvement (bargaining leverage), and (2) she may reduce the 'lost profits' component of the dominant patentee's damages because the dominant patentee would not have fully replaced infringer's sales that were based on the improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse doctrine of equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a defendant's device literally falls within the claims but has 'so far changed the principle of the device that the claims of the patent, literally construed, have ceased to represent his actual invention,' the defendant may be excused from infringement (the 'reverse' doctrine of equivalents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied rarely; courts ask whether the accused product is 'so far changed in principle' or performs in a 'substantially different way' (Westinghouse/Boyden example; SRI v. Matsushita discussed). Trial courts must often make factual determinations about whether the device is sufficiently changed in principle to warrant the defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance-of-improvement test for equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: The more significant the technological advance represented by the allegedly infringing device, the less willing courts should be to find it an equivalent of the patentee's device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rationale helps explain when reverse equivalents (and perhaps doctrine of equivalents) should protect improvers from holdup; courts should consider technical merits and whether the accused device performs substantially differently or departs from the patentee's principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement concern with very broad claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Broad claims that encompass embodiments which can be made only after significant additional research raise special concerns: such breadth may cover later, substantial improvements not contemplated at filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases like Westinghouse/Boyden illustrate that even if literal claim language could read on later inventions, courts may refuse to find infringement if the later invention is a 'manifest departure from the principle of the ... patent.' Enablement/claim breadth issues thus inform infringement analysis and reverse equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic assessment of improvement patents and holdup
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether issuing an improvement patent (or allowing broad pioneer patents) is efficient depends on the relative contributions of the original invention and the improvement to the 'original plus improvement' combination; if the original contributes little, the holdup problem may be significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where original and improvement contribute roughly equal value, issuing an improvement patent may be reasonable; where the improvement supplies most of the value, the original patentee's holdup power can be inefficient. Reverse doctrine of equivalents can mitigate holdup by excusing improvers from infringement liability in some cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent policy tradeoff: incentives versus deadweight costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional analysis focuses on the tradeoff between providing inventive incentives (longer/more extensive coverage) and the deadweight costs from monopoly (underuse of the invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many models (Nordhaus; Gilbert & Shapiro; Klemperer) analyze optimal patent life and breadth via this tradeoff, but the article argues these are insufficient unless they incorporate multiactor/dynamic effects (how patent scope affects subsequent inventive activity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of multiactor dynamics (common-pool and race models)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent scope decisions should account for multi-actor, multi-round invention processes (e.g., 'fishing from a common pool' or 'race to patent'), because rivalry among inventors can generate inefficiencies but also spur useful exploration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Static single-actor analyses miss how broad patents affect whether substitutes and follow-on inventions are created and how efficiently. Models that incorporate rivalry show robust inefficiencies from rivalrous efforts, but policy must weigh these against the benefits of competition in invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kitch's prospect theory and its limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Kitch analogized patents to mining claims: patents grant a prospect allowing a single right-holder to coordinate development, mitigate duplication, and potentially be more efficient than rivalry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique: centralized control often underdevelops parts of the prospect, suffers from cognitive and organizational limits, and licensing tailored coordination is costly. Empirical evidence suggests rivalry often produces broader exploration than centralized control; transaction costs and licensing frictions make Kitch's idealized coordination unlikely in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry-specific models of technical advance (discrete, cumulative, chemical, science-based)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical advance differs by industry; the paper identifies four models: (1) discrete invention, (2) cumulative technologies, (3) chemical technologies (mixed features), and (4) science-based technologies—each implying different patent-scope concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For discrete inventions, broad control of a particular invention is less likely to hinder others. For cumulative technologies (automobiles, semiconductors, computers), broad pioneer patents or multiple broad patents on components can create blocking and substantially affect subsequent development. Chemical and science-based technologies have their own special considerations (licensing traditions in chemical industries, and concentrated races and danger of overbroad scope in science-based fields).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment questions for patent-scope effects in cumulative technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: When analyzing cumulative technologies, ask: (1) What are the consequences of 'pioneer' patents? (2) How do broad patents on components affect subsequent development?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper focuses on impact on subsequent innovation rather than whether a patent should have been granted at all, and accepts that claiming the general inventive principle may be justified but asks how breadth alters the environment for follow-on development (historical examples: Selden patent, Edison).

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical and policy criterion: speed of innovation matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Premise: when it comes to invention and innovation, faster introduction of improvements is socially preferable because R&D increases inventions which raise productivity and welfare; earlier availability accelerates follow-on improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This assumption aligns with patent law's procedural preferences (priority to first to invent, early reduction to practice, provisions encouraging early filing). Thus policy and judicial doctrines should consider how scope decisions affect the timing of improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transaction costs and practical limits on coordinating development via licensing
rubrics_metrics.description: High transaction costs, especially for tailored licenses, make it difficult for a broad patent holder to orchestrate R&D through selective licensing; broadly identical licenses are easier but unlikely to achieve the nuanced coordination Kitch envisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical research cited finds no cases where a holder of a broad patent effectively used tailored licensing to coordinate R&D. This supports limiting patent breadth when coordination cannot realistically be achieved through licensing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy to property/mining law as a rationale for limiting scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Just as mining and mineral claim systems limit claim boundaries and require active work to prevent hoarding/speculation, patent doctrines should limit breadth to prevent overly broad exclusion that preempts valuable follow-on work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The legal analogy suggests practical mechanisms (requirements to work claims, limits on breadth) that constrain speculative or hoarding behavior; policy should aim for a regime protecting improvers' bargaining position relative to pioneers.
